title: White Winemaking in Burgundy
description: The art and science behind Burgundy's world-renowned Chardonnay whites — from press to bottle.
lessons.0.title: Harvesting and Pressing White Grapes
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Harvesting and Pressing White Grapes
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: How Chardonnay is harvested and pressed in Burgundy — critical decisions that set the quality ceiling for every white wine.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Timing the Harvest for White Grapes
lessons.0.slides.1.content: For Chardonnay, harvest timing involves an additional dimension compared to reds: acidity preservation. Chardonnay loses acidity quickly as it ripens, and the ideal harvest window — maximum flavour with sufficient freshness — can last only a few days.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Early harvest: higher acidity, green apple, citrus character — more minerally, austere style
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Late harvest: higher sugar, tropical fruit, melon character — rounder, richer style
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: The ideal: balanced ripeness with enough acid for ageing — the goal of Chablis, Puligny and Meursault
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Climate change: modern Burgundy whites are now often picked 2–3 weeks earlier than in the 1990s to preserve acidity
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🔧 Whole-Cluster Pressing (Pressurage Entier)
lessons.0.slides.2.content: For white wines, whole-cluster pressing — pressing intact bunches without destemming — is standard practice in Burgundy. Unlike red winemaking, the goal is to extract juice without colour or tannin from the grape skins.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Whole-cluster pressing: minimises skin contact, producing cleaner, more delicate juice
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Gentle pressing: multiple low-pressure cycles extract juice progressively; harsh pressure avoided
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Press fractions: first press (best quality) vs later press fractions (lower quality, more phenolic)
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Free-run juice (vin de goutte): the finest fraction; most aromatic and delicate
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 🧊 Settling (Débourbage) and Clarification
lessons.0.slides.3.content: After pressing, the juice (moût) is settled cold (débourbage) to allow solid particles — grape solids, skin fragments — to sink before fermentation begins.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Cold settling: juice held at 5–10°C for 12–24 hours; solids sink by gravity
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Level of clarification is a stylistic choice: very clean juice = more precise, mineral wine; slightly turbid juice = more texture
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Too much clarification: removes beneficial fine lees that add texture to the finished wine
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Modern trend: lighter, less aggressive clarification to preserve naturally occurring fine lees
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Harvest timing for Chardonnay is critical — acidity preservation is as important as sugar ripeness
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Whole-cluster pressing is standard for Burgundy whites — it produces cleaner, more mineral juice
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Cold settling before fermentation removes unwanted solids but preserves quality fine lees
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Press fractions must be carefully evaluated — only the best portions are used for top cuvées
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why must Chardonnay be harvested at exactly the right moment?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. To avoid competition with other grape varieties
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Chardonnay loses acidity rapidly as it ripens, and the ideal balance of flavour and freshness lasts only a few days
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. AOC rules mandate a single harvest date for all Chardonnay
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Mechanical harvesting is only permitted on specific dates
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Chardonnay is particularly sensitive to harvest timing. As it ripens, total acidity drops while sugar rises. The window of ideal balance — enough sugar for body and flavour complexity, enough acidity for freshness and ageing potential — can be extremely narrow, sometimes just 3–5 days in warm years.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is the key advantage of whole-cluster pressing for white wine?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. It extracts maximum tannin and colour for richer wines
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. It minimises skin contact, producing cleaner, more mineral and delicate juice
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. It is faster and less labour-intensive than destemming
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. It extracts more sugar, raising the potential alcohol
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Whole-cluster pressing for white wines (unlike red whole-cluster fermentation) aims to extract clean juice with minimal skin contact. The skins contain phenolics and colour — unwanted in a fine white wine. Gentle pressing of intact clusters extracts the most delicate, mineral juice.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is 'débourbage'?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. The addition of selected yeasts to start fermentation
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Cold settling of freshly pressed juice to allow grape solids to sink before fermentation
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. Removal of barrels from the cellar for cleaning
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Débourbage is the cold settling of freshly pressed juice, typically at 5–10°C for 12–24 hours. Grape solids (pulp, skin fragments) sink by gravity, leaving cleaner juice above. The clean juice is then racked off the solids and transferred to fermentation vessels.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.question: Why might a winemaker choose slightly turbid (less clarified) juice for fermentation?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. Turbid juice ferments faster and produces higher alcohol
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Slightly more solids in the juice produce a rounder, more textural wine during fermentation
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Turbid juice requires less sulphur and is therefore more natural
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Regulations require a minimum level of turbidity for Grand Cru wines
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Very aggressive clarification removes fine lees (bâtonnage substrate) and grape solids that contribute texture and mouthfeel during fermentation. Some producers prefer lighter clarification, accepting slightly turbid juice to preserve these elements and produce a rounder, more textural style.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.question: How has climate change affected Chardonnay harvest timing in Burgundy?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. Harvests are now 2–3 weeks earlier than in the 1990s to preserve acidity
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Harvests are now 2–3 weeks later to achieve full phenolic ripeness
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Harvest dates have not changed significantly
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. Higher temperatures allow two harvests per year
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Rising temperatures in Burgundy have accelerated grape ripening significantly. Average harvest dates are now 2–3 weeks earlier than they were in the 1990s, reflecting earlier véraison and faster sugar accumulation. Producers pick earlier to preserve natural acidity and freshness in the wines.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Harvesting and pressing are the foundational decisions for Burgundy white wines. The clarity, freshness and precision that define great Chablis, Meursault and Montrachet begin not in the cellar but in the vineyard and at the press.
lessons.1.title: Barrel Fermentation and Bâtonnage
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Barrel Fermentation and Bâtonnage
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: The defining technique of white Burgundy — fermenting and aging in barrel — and how stirring the lees creates the signature creamy, complex texture.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Why Ferment in Barrel?
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Top white Burgundy — from Meursault to Montrachet — is typically fermented in oak barrel rather than in stainless steel tanks. Barrel fermentation integrates oak more seamlessly and produces a fundamentally different texture.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Integration: oak flavours integrate more smoothly when fermentation occurs in the barrel rather than in a tank
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Texture: the yeast cells interact with wood surface, creating a creamier, more complex mouthfeel
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Micro-oxygenation: fermentation in wood provides gentle oxidative contact through barrel staves
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Temperature: fermentation generates heat; the small barrel (228L) naturally limits temperature peaks
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🥢 Bâtonnage (Lees Stirring)
lessons.1.slides.2.content: After fermentation, dead yeast cells (lees) settle to the bottom of the barrel. Bâtonnage — stirring these lees back into suspension — is one of Burgundy's signature techniques for white wines.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Purpose: lees release polysaccharides, amino acids and fatty acids that add creaminess and texture
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Frequency: typically weekly in the first months, tapering off as the lees become exhausted
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Duration: bâtonnage continues for 6–12 months depending on the cuvée and vintage
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Effect: adds roundness, body, complexity and a characteristic 'lees' nutty richness
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.4: Risk: excessive bâtonnage in warm vintages can cause reduction (sulphur off-notes)
lessons.1.slides.3.title: New Oak and White Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.3.content: The percentage of new oak barrels used for white wines shapes flavour profile dramatically. The trend in modern Burgundy is toward less new oak — expressing terroir more cleanly.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Chablis: traditionally no oak at all (stainless steel); 'old oak' used at most
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Premier and Grand Cru: 30–50% new oak at traditional estates; 10–20% at modern producers
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Debate: old-school Burgundy used 100% new oak for Grand Cru whites; new generation drastically reducing
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Barrel fermentation creates more seamless oak integration and richer texture than tank-fermented white wine
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Bâtonnage is Burgundy's signature technique — it adds the characteristic creamy richness of great Meursault
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 New oak percentages are falling across Burgundy — the trend is toward purer terroir expression
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Chablis is typically unoaked or very lightly oaked — its style depends entirely on mineral terroir
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is bâtonnage?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Pressing the grape skins after red wine fermentation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Stirring the dead yeast lees back into suspension in the barrel during white wine aging
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Racking wine from one barrel to another
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Adding sugar (chaptalization) to raise potential alcohol
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Bâtonnage (lees stirring) uses a bâton (stick) or rotating barrel mechanism to stir dead yeast cells back into the wine from the bottom of the barrel. The lees release polysaccharides, amino acids and fatty acids that add creaminess, body and complexity — the source of great Meursault's signature richness.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.question: Why does barrel fermentation produce better oak integration than tank fermentation with barrel aging?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Barrels are made of thicker wood than tanks
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Oak compounds integrate more seamlessly when released during active fermentation, becoming part of the wine's structure
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Tank fermentation requires more sulphur additions
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Fermentation temperature is lower in barrels
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: When fermentation occurs inside the barrel, oak-derived compounds (vanillin, tannins, toasty flavours) are incorporated gradually into the fermenting wine as yeast activity is high — they become structurally integrated rather than added on top. The result is seamless rather than obvious oak character.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is the main risk of excessive bâtonnage in warm vintages?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. The wine becomes too alcoholic
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Reduction — the production of sulphur off-notes from disturbing lees too aggressively
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. The wine loses too much colour
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. The barrels crack from the agitation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Excessive bâtonnage — particularly in warm vintages when lees are metabolically active — can produce hydrogen sulphide and mercaptans (reduction), creating unpleasant sulphurous or rubbery off-notes. Skilled winemakers reduce bâtonnage frequency as the vintage temperature rises and lees activity intensifies.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.question: What is the typical approach to oak for Chablis Grand Cru?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. 100% new oak for maximum richness
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Steel tank fermentation with no oak contact
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Old neutral oak or steel — to let the pure mineral terroir speak without wood flavour
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. A blend of new and old oak, the same as Meursault
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Chablis's identity is built on Kimmeridgian limestone soil and cool climate — not oak. The majority of Chablis producers (including most Grand Cru estates) use stainless steel or old neutral oak to let the mineral, oyster-shell and citrus terroir character speak without being masked by wood flavours.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.question: What compounds do lees release during bâtonnage that add texture to the wine?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Polysaccharides, amino acids and fatty acids that add creaminess and body
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Acetic acid and volatile compounds
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. Sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Dead yeast cells (lees) undergo autolysis — they break down and release polysaccharides, mannoproteins, amino acids and fatty acids into the wine. These compounds coat the palate, add creamy texture, body and a characteristic nutty, yeasty complexity. This is the source of white Burgundy's famous richness.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Barrel fermentation and bâtonnage are the twin pillars of white Burgundy's style. They transform the linear acidity and mineral character of Chardonnay into the complex, creamy, textured white wines that have made Meursault and Montrachet legendary.
lessons.2.title: Malolactic Fermentation (MLF)
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Malolactic Fermentation (MLF)
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 10 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Malolactic fermentation's profound role in shaping the style and texture of Burgundy white wines — and why some producers now block it.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: What Is Malolactic Fermentation?
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a bacterial transformation (not a true fermentation) that converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid. It dramatically changes a wine's texture, acidity and flavour profile.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Malic acid: naturally present in grapes; sharp, tart, green apple character
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Lactic acid: softer, creamier; associated with dairy and buttery notes
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: MLF also produces diacetyl — the compound responsible for buttery character in Chardonnay
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: MLF is standard in Burgundy white winemaking; most wines go through complete MLF
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Effects of MLF on Burgundy White Wine
lessons.2.slides.2.content: MLF changes white wine fundamentally — reducing acidity, adding roundness and contributing distinct aromatic notes.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Lower total acidity: pH rises, wine tastes softer and rounder
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Creamy texture: lactic acid and diacetyl add a dairy quality to the mouthfeel
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Aromatic shift: green apple and citrus notes reduce; butterscotch, hazelnut, cream notes emerge
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Greater stability: MLF uses up malic acid, preventing re-fermentation in bottle
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Blocking MLF: The Modern Approach
lessons.2.slides.3.content: With the challenge of maintaining freshness and acidity in warm vintages, a growing number of producers — especially in Chablis — are partially or fully blocking MLF.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Blocking technique: cool cellar temperatures or SO₂ additions to suppress lactic acid bacteria
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Result: higher natural acidity is preserved; crisper, more mineral and citrus-forward style
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: William Fèvre (Chablis): famous for blocking MLF to preserve Chablis's signature piercing acidity
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Trade-off: without MLF, wines need longer in bottle to integrate their higher acidity
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 MLF converts sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid, fundamentally softening Burgundy whites
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 The 'buttery' character in Chardonnay comes from diacetyl produced during MLF
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Some producers block MLF to preserve freshness and mineral acidity in warmer vintages
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 MLF is standard in Burgundy but optional — it is a fundamental stylistic choice
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.question: What chemical transformation occurs during malolactic fermentation (MLF)?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Glucose is converted to ethanol and CO₂
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Sharp malic acid is converted by bacteria into softer lactic acid
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Sulphur dioxide is converted into sulphur compounds
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Tartaric acid is converted into carbonic acid
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: MLF is conducted by lactic acid bacteria (LAB), most commonly Oenococcus oeni. These bacteria decarboxylate malic acid (sharp, tart) into lactic acid (soft, creamy) and CO₂. This transformation softens the wine's texture and acidity profile, moving away from crisp/acidic toward round/creamy.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.question: What compound produced during MLF is responsible for 'buttery' aromas in Chardonnay?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Diacetyl (produced by lactic acid bacteria during MLF)
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Malic acid remaining after fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Esters produced during primary fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Diacetyl is a by-product of the MLF process produced by lactic acid bacteria. At low concentrations it adds a pleasant buttery or creamy note; at high concentrations it becomes a dominant 'movie popcorn' butter fault. Modern Burgundy producers calibrate MLF to achieve subtle richness, not overt butteriness.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.question: Why do some Chablis producers block malolactic fermentation?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. MLF makes Chablis too expensive to produce
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. To preserve Chablis's signature high acidity, mineral freshness and citrus character
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. French law prohibits MLF in Chablis
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. To reduce the wine's alcohol content
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Chablis's distinctive identity is built on its piercing, mineral acidity from Kimmeridgian limestone soils. MLF, by converting malic to lactic acid, softens that signature sharpness. Producers like William Fèvre block MLF (via cold temperatures and SO₂) to preserve the taut, mineral, oyster-shell character that defines classic Chablis.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.question: What is the main trade-off when blocking MLF?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. The wine becomes too expensive to produce
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Wines with higher residual malic acid need longer bottle aging to integrate their sharpness
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Blocked-MLF wines cannot be exported
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Blocking MLF produces a permanent sulphur taint
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Wines that have not gone through MLF retain higher malic acid, making them taste sharper and more astringent in youth. They need extended bottle time to soften and integrate. This is acceptable — even desirable — for long-lived Grand Cru whites, but may be a challenge for early-drinking village wines.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.question: Which aromatic change is associated with completed MLF in Chardonnay?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. Green apple and lemon notes become more pronounced
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. The wine loses all aromatic character
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Green apple and citrus notes reduce; butterscotch, hazelnut and cream notes emerge
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. The wine develops pronounced tropical fruit character
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: MLF shifts the aromatic profile of Chardonnay from the primary fruit character of malic acid (green apple, lemon, citrus) toward secondary lactic notes (butterscotch, cream, hazelnut). Combined with oak and lees contact, this transformation creates the multi-layered complexity of great white Burgundy.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.2.slides.6.content: Malolactic fermentation is not just a technical step — it is a fundamental stylistic choice that defines whether a Burgundy white is crisply mineral or voluptuously rich. The growing debate over whether to pursue full, partial or no MLF reflects producers' responses to a warming climate.
lessons.3.title: Aging, Assembly and Bottling
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Aging, Assembly and Bottling
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 10 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: The final stages of white Burgundy production — élevage, fining and filtration decisions, and the timing of bottling.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: ⏳ Élevage Duration for White Wines
lessons.3.slides.1.content: White Burgundy's élevage (raising of the wine) spans the period from the end of fermentation to bottling, during which bâtonnage, MLF and gradual oxidative development all occur in barrel.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Village wines: typically 10–12 months of barrel aging
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Bottling timing: later bottling = more complexity; earlier bottling = more freshness and fruit purity
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🔍 Fining and Filtration
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Before bottling, the winemaker decides whether to fine and/or filter — critical decisions affecting texture, stability and the wine's expression of terroir.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Fining: adding bentonite (clay) or albumin (egg white) to attract and precipitate protein or phenolic particles
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Filtration: passing wine through a membrane to remove microbes and particles
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Risk of excessive fining/filtration: strips texture, body and complexity from the wine
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Natural wine trend: many top estates now bottle without fining or filtration (non-filtré, non-collé)
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.3.points.0: 🍷 Élevage duration varies by appellation level — Grand Cru white wines spend up to 24 months in barrel
lessons.3.slides.3.points.1: 🍷 Fining and filtration are declining at top estates — unfined and unfiltered is increasingly the norm
lessons.3.slides.3.points.2: 🍷 Bottling timing involves a balance between freshness and complexity
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: 🍷 The combination of barrel fermentation + bâtonnage + MLF + oak aging defines classic white Burgundy style
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.0.question: How long is a typical Grand Cru white Burgundy aged in barrel?
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.0.explanati: Grand Cru white Burgundy — such as Le Montrachet or Corton-Charlemagne — is typically aged in barrel for 15–24 months. This extended élevage period allows full integration of MLF, oak and bâtonnage effects, building the textural complexity and aging potential that defines great white Burgundy.
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.1.question: What does 'non-filtré, non-collé' on a label indicate?
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.1.options.0: A. The wine has not been aged in barrel
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.1.options.1: B. The wine has not been fined or filtered before bottling
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.1.options.3: D. The wine comes from ungrafted vines
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.1.explanati: Non-filtré (unfiltered) and non-collé (unfined) indicate the wine has been bottled without these clarification treatments. Many top Burgundy estates believe fining and filtration strip texture and complexity. Unfined, unfiltered wines may occasionally throw a light sediment or show slight haze — this is natural and harmless.
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.2.question: What is bentonite used for in white winemaking?
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.2.options.0: A. To add texture and creaminess during bâtonnage
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.2.options.1: B. As a fining agent to remove unstable proteins that could cause haze in bottle
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.2.options.2: C. As a natural acidifier in warm vintages
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.2.explanati: Bentonite is a clay fining agent that carries a negative charge and attracts positively charged proteins in white wine. These proteins, if left in the wine, can combine with heat to form a haze or precipitate in bottle. Bentonite addition causes the proteins to flocculate and settle, which are then removed by racking.
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.question: What is the trade-off when a winemaker bottles Grand Cru white Burgundy later rather than earlier?
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.options.0: A. Later bottling always results in higher alcohol
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.options.1: B. Later bottling adds more complexity but may reduce primary fruit freshness
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.options.2: C. Earlier bottling produces a more complex wine
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.options.3: D. Bottling time has no effect on wine quality
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.3.explanati: Extended élevage (barrel aging) allows greater complexity from oak, lees and oxidative development to build in the wine — but it comes at the cost of primary fruit freshness. The winemaker judges when the balance between built complexity and retained freshness is optimal for the intended style.
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.question: What defines the 'classic white Burgundy style'?
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.options.0: A. Tank fermentation, no bâtonnage, no MLF, no oak
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.options.1: B. Barrel fermentation + bâtonnage + MLF + oak aging — creating creamy texture with terroir expression
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.options.2: C. 100% new oak, no bâtonnage, blocked MLF
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.options.3: D. Cold fermentation in stainless steel with 100% new oak aging
lessons.3.slides.4.questions.4.explanati: Classic white Burgundy style is defined by the combination of barrel fermentation (seamless oak integration), bâtonnage (creaminess from lees contact), full malolactic fermentation (softened acidity and lactic richness) and extended barrel aging (oxidative complexity) — creating wines of extraordinary texture, depth and longevity.
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.5.content: White Burgundy production is a cascade of interconnected decisions — each affecting the final wine's texture, aromatic profile and ageing capacity. The greatest whites of Meursault, Puligny and Chablis achieve their transcendent character not from a single technique but from the perfect calibration of all these elements together.
